briefing.question: What does a nation owe the stranger at its door, and who decides: the executive in a crisis, or the law Congress already wrote?
briefing.agreed: A nation may guard its border but may not send the stranger to danger unheard.
briefing.split: Kant, refuge a right; Vattel, good reason; Hobbes, locate the judge; Locke, prerogative fills gaps; Madison, each branch its own.

briefing.question: Who guards the guardians? Should judges answer to the people's representatives for how they rule, or does justice require that they answer to no one but the law?
briefing.agreed: Judges answer for abuse of office, not for how they read the law.
briefing.split: Hamilton, usurpation only; Jefferson, the people judge; Lincoln, argue and win elections; Aristotle, law is reason.

briefing.question: Is loyalty owed first to a leader and his agenda, or to the institution and the rules that outlast any one leader?
briefing.agreed: Senate consent is part of the design; today's precedent serves the other side later.
briefing.split: Hamilton, a stopgap; Madison, ambition guards; Burke, judgment owed; Washington, institutions over a chief.

briefing.question: Can a shared public institution be neutral, and is neutrality itself a moral stance? Where is the line between dignity and advocacy?
briefing.agreed: No institution is value-free; equal standing may be affirmed, live disputes aired.
briefing.split: Rawls, standing not sides; MacIntyre, defend your tradition; Rousseau, few common signs; Mill, open argument.

briefing.question: Is the best answer to evil to bury its words or to study them? Does understanding a poison protect people from it, or spread it?
briefing.agreed: Evil must be understood to be resisted; framing and timing matter.
briefing.split: Milton, refute it; Mill, no ban; Plato, guard the young; Santayana, study as memory; Wiesel, let the victims be heard.

briefing.question: Is justice mainly about material conditions or about recognition and dignity, and can a movement pursue both without losing its center?
briefing.agreed: Material conditions stay central; some harms to dignity are material.
briefing.split: Marx, wages first; Nietzsche, who profits from suffering; Lasch, dignity in work; Fraser, equal participation.

briefing.question: What do Christians owe to fellow believers across political lines, and how should a state weigh security against the free exchange of witness and ideas?
briefing.agreed: States may control entry for real reasons; believers owe each other a hearing.
briefing.split: Augustine, one pilgrim city; Vattel, mastery with reason; Mill, listeners robbed; Holmes, hear the critics.

briefing.question: Is human nature a given to be received or something each person defines? And can a teaching about the body be both true and gentle?
briefing.agreed: Difference never justifies subordination; truth must be spoken with love.
briefing.split: Aquinas, partnership; John Paul II, mutual gift; Beauvoir, no fixed destiny; Wollstonecraft, no rule over minds; Augustine, love.

briefing.question: Is public faith a private matter that should stay off the pitch, or a part of the person that a free society must make room for, even when it unsettles others?
briefing.agreed: The state stays out; one standard for every faith; bear what unsettles.
briefing.split: Locke, even restraint; Williams, judge no faith; Murray, argue openly; Neuhaus, a naked square gets filled.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Kant speaks first because his Third Definitive Article of Perpetual Peace is the classic philosophical statement of what a stranger may claim on arrival, and it already contains the idea behind the modern rule against sending people back to danger. Vattel follows because the report names his Law of Nations as the case for a sovereign's control of entry, and he also wrote on the exile's claim to dwell somewhere; the only English texts of his book that could be fetched here are eighteenth-century scans with unreliable long-s OCR, so he is paraphrased. Hobbes is seated because the report names him for the state's first duty of self-protection and the sovereign as judge of what defense requires. Locke follows because the report names him for the rule of law, and his chapter on prerogative is the classic treatment of when an executive may act beyond or against a statute in an emergency. Madison closes because the report names Federalist No. 47 on the separation of powers. Exodus 22:21, which the report also names, is read by the moderator rather than given a chair; the parable of the Good Samaritan is noted but not quoted. The justices, the President, the reporter, the challengers, and the commentators named in the report are context only.

closing.text: Where they agreed: a nation may control its border, but it owes the stranger at least freedom from being sent to death or danger without a hearing of some kind, and the hard question is which branch may decide how. Where they split: Kant makes refuge from death a right, not a kindness. Vattel gives the nation first judgment yet denies it may refuse the endangered exile without cause. Hobbes would give the judge of safety broad power but wants it plainly located. Locke allows emergency prerogative only where the law failed to foresee the case. Madison asks the Court to keep each branch to its own power and sends policy disputes back to Congress.

turn.text: I began by insisting that “We are speaking here, as in the previous articles, not of philanthropy, but of right” (Perpetual Peace, Third Definitive Article) The stranger's claim is not a favor the host may grant or withhold by mood. In my words, “hospitality signifies the claim of a stranger entering foreign territory to be treated by its owner without hostility.” (Perpetual Peace, Third Definitive Article) That is a narrow right, not a right to settle. I did not say every nation must admit every arrival as a resident, and the supporters are right that a host may set terms.

I held that every sovereign may forbid entry to its territory, either generally or to particular persons, when the safety of the state requires it, and that it alone judges, in the first instance, whether its circumstances allow it to receive more people (The Law of Nations, paraphrased). The supporters who say a nation must be able to close its door in an emergency are standing on my ground.

But he also held that an exile keeps a right to live somewhere and may not be refused without good reason, so the power to close the border is not unlimited.

works: Leviathan (1651), Part II, chs. XVIII and XXX

turn.text: Vattel softens the sovereign's power; I would not. The commonwealth exists for one purpose: “The OFFICE of the Soveraign, (be it a Monarch, or an Assembly,) consisteth in the end, for which he was trusted with the Soveraign Power, namely the procuration of the Safety Of The People” (Leviathan, Part II, ch. XXX) And because whoever is given the end must be given the means, “it belongeth of Right, to whatsoever Man, or Assembly that hath the Soveraignty, to be Judge both of the meanes of Peace and Defence; and also of the hindrances, and disturbances of the same” (Leviathan, Part II, ch. XVIII) That is the strongest case the supporters can make. If the people's safety is the end, someone must be able to judge quickly what threatens it, and a flood of arrivals is the kind of disturbance I meant.

turn.text: Locke has brought us to the separation of powers, and I wrote the standard warning: “The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands, whether of one, a few, or many, and whether hereditary, self-appointed, or elective, may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.” (Federalist No. 47) I did not mean that the branches never touch. I meant that no one of them should hold the whole of another's power. A president who could repeal a statute by declaring an emergency would hold the legislative power; a court that set immigration policy would do the same from the other side.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: can a shared public institution be neutral, is neutrality itself a moral stance, and where is the line between dignity and advocacy? opening.text: Tonight's subject: is justice mainly about material conditions or about recognition and dignity, and can a movement pursue both without losing its center? The report gives one side as supporters, including a British academic, who say the professor is right that much of the left stopped fighting for better wages, housing, and infrastructure and started policing language and feelings instead, and that working-class voters notice when a movement cares more about symbols than about their bills. The other side is critics, who answer that the left still pushes for redistribution and that it is the right that keeps starting culture-war fights, and who say identity and material life cannot be neatly separated: discrimination and trauma have economic costs, and naming harm is not a distraction from justice but part of it. Marx, the report begins with your materialism. Begin.

chairs.name: Nancy Fraser
works: Redistribution or Recognition? (with Axel Honneth, 2003), paraphrased

turn.text: Lasch and Marx put the material first; I asked whether we must choose. I argued that justice has at least two dimensions, the redistribution of resources and the recognition of status, and that many groups suffer both maldistribution and misrecognition at once, so neither can be reduced to the other (Redistribution or Recognition?, paraphrased). That is the critics' point: harm to dignity can have economic costs, and poverty is itself a kind of disrespect.

turn.text: I described the Church as a people on pilgrimage inside every earthly state. “This heavenly city, then, while it sojourns on earth, calls citizens out of all nations, and gathers together a society of pilgrims of all languages” (City of God XIX.17) Its members are bound to one another before they are bound to any nation's alliances. A Christian in Washington and a Christian in Bethlehem belong to one city, and the suffering of one is the concern of the other. That is the critics' claim, and on its own ground it is sound.

The state may decide who crosses its border. What believers may not do is let an earthly alliance decide whose suffering they are willing to hear. turn.text: But I also held that this right should be exercised for real reasons of safety and the good of the nation, not from caprice, and that the duties of humanity bind nations toward one another, including openness to harmless passage and exchange (The Law of Nations, paraphrased). John Courtney Murray is seated because the report names him for pluralism in the shared public square; his works are in copyright, so he is paraphrased. opening.text: Tonight's subject: is public faith a private matter that should stay off the pitch, or a part of the person that a free society must make room for, even when it unsettles others? The report names the image behind the gesture: “The four and twenty elders fall down before him that sat on the throne, and worship him that liveth for ever and ever, and cast their crowns before the throne” (Revelation 4:10) The report gives one side as many Christians and free-speech defenders, who see a double standard, since rainbow armbands and Ramadan greetings were no problem but a Christian goal celebration is, and who say a player humbly laying his crown before Christ harms no one and that pressuring him to stop is a quiet form of religious discrimination. Locke, the report begins with toleration. Begin.
